newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma commentary says Suu Kyi party greedy, doomed.
newsitem.headline: Burma commentary says Suu Kyi party greedy, doomed.

text.p: Official Burmese newspapers on Friday accused Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy (NLD) of being power-hungry and said it was doomed to failure.

An editorial published in both state-run Burmese-language newspapers likened the NLD to the outlawed Burma Communist Party (BCP), saying the NLD's repeated demand for dialogue with the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) was only so it could eventually seize power.
Burma's official newspapers are considered to be the mouthpieces of the military government.
"The basic ambition of Suu Kyi and groups who are demanding dialogue with the SLORC is not for 'national consolidation' nor 'democracy'," the editorial said.
"The dialogue Suu Kyi and groups are demanding is just like the demand of the fallen Burma Communist Party. It is only for seizing state power."
The BCP was a major armed insurgent group but was outlawed in 1948 after independence from Britain.
The editorial said Suu Kyi's party must be opposed and punished by the entire nation.
"They will meet with a terrible fate and they are doomed to fall."
The NLD, co-founded by Suu Kyi in 1988 amid anti-government protests, won a landslide victory in a 1990 election. It has never taken power because the SLORC never recognised the results of the poll.

Suu Kyi, the 1991 Nobel Peace laureate who was released from six years of house arrest in July 1995, has repeatedly called on the SLORC to hold a dialogue with the NLD and ethnic groups to figure out a way to bring democracy to Burma.

The SLORC has refused dialogue, saying the only forum for discussion on the future of Burma's government is through the National Convention -- a group of mostly handpicked delegates who have been meeting intermittently since 1993 to draft guidelines for a new constitution.

Suu Kyi angered the SLORC in November 1995 when she pulled the NLD out of the convention, saying it did not represent the will of the people. Top NLD officials are currently drafting their own version of a constitution.
A top Burmese official said on Thursday restrictions would remain on Suu Kyi and some universities would stay closed following student unrest last month.
Senior intelligence official Colonel Thein Swe told Reuters the decision requiring Suu Kyi to inform the government of her movements and visitors was aimed to protect, not inconvenience, her.
Suu Kyi told Reuters in a telephone interview on Thursday it was "very silly" to presume the restrictions were imposed for her benefit.
